description.en:
Ontology capturing the legal landscape governing AI-driven automated
        decision-making in medical contexts. Covers CJEU precedents on GDPR
        Art.22, UPC/EPO patent litigation in MedTech, the EU AI Act high-risk
        regime, MDR 2017/745, PLD 2024/2853, EHDS 2025/327, DGA 2022/868,
        and Data Act 2023/2854 — with full precedent chains, SHACL runtime
        constraints, and compliance obligation mappings.
        Imports: W3C DPV v2.0 (data privacy vocabulary), AIRO (AI risk ontology),
        ELI (European Legislation Identifier), ECLI (European Case Law Identifier).

comments.en: Version 5.1.0: corrective release consolidating four rounds of work, none previously deployed. (1) All nine CJEU paragraph citations were re-checked and all nine corrected; two substantive mischaracterisations were removed (the health-status exclusion is categorical under PNR Directive Art.6(4), not curable by a GDPR Art.9(2) basis; the strict-necessity test does not entail invalidity, the Court having upheld the Directive by Charter-conforming interpretation). (2) The patent, EPO and UPC instances were verified: T 1191/19 re-dated and its holding rewritten, T 0161/18 corrected to a refused application, the citesPrecedent graph repaired, litigation statuses refreshed. (3) Legislative citations were audited: all four EHDS articles carried proposal numbering and were renumbered, Art.73 was added, PLD Art.11 was corrected from the causation presumption to exemption from liability, DGA Art.31 was corrected to Art.29, and AI Act Art.50 was relabelled. (4) MAILO's boundaries were made explicit: every case now declares an InclusionBasis and every principle an EncodingBasis, separating what a court held from what the ontology designer inferred or operationalised. Correcting the hierarchy that let the boundary errors pass, AutomatedDecisionSystem is no longer a subclass of MedicalAISystem — the entailment ran backwards, making every automated decision system medical. Parts IV and V of the SHACL shapes now enforce citation integrity and boundary declaration on the graph itself, and each shape has been tested against the error it was written for.

abstract.value: MAILO (Medical AI Legal Ontology) is a machine-executable knowledge graph encoding EU regulatory obligations for medical artificial intelligence systems. It formalises eight EU legislative instruments -- the GDPR, MDR, AI Act, Product Liability Directive, EHDS, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and Trade Secrets Directive -- as OWL 2 classes and SHACL shape constraints, grounded in three CJEU judgments on automated decision-making (Ligue des droits humains, SCHUFA Holding, and Dun & Bradstreet Austria). MAILO functions as a deterministic, auditable compliance-verification layer: SHACL NodeShapes validate instance data describing a medical AI system against the encoded legal constraints and produce structured, traceable conformance reports.

comment.en: The system is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment. MDR and IVDR are in Annex I Section A, so Class IIa, IIb and III medical devices incorporating AI take this route automatically. Art.86 and Art.26(11), both scoped to Annex III, DO NOT APPLY. Obligations for this route apply from 2 August 2028.

Encoding basis (DesignerOperationalisation): Para 61 requires the data subject to understand which personal data were used and in what way. identifiesInputFactors is MAILO's predicate for that standard.
Encoding basis (DesignerOperationalisation): Paras 49-50 state a determining-role test. The substantive-oversight predicate is MAILO's proxy for it; the Court set no rubber-stamping standard.
A 'decision' under Art.22 encompasses any act producing legal or similarly significant effects. Automated scoring creating probabilities relied upon by third parties constitutes a 'decision'.
Any positive match from automated PNR analysis must be subject to individual non-automated review before any measure is taken. Establishes constitutional minimum for meaningful human intervention.

C-201/14 Bara: personal data transferred between public administrative bodies and further processed require that data subjects be informed of the transfer and of the categories of data concerned. UNVERIFIED (v5.2.0): no paragraph anchor and no ECLI are recorded, and the holding has not been checked against the judgment text. Do not cite until verified.

Encoding basis (DesignerOperationalisation): The characterisation of Art.22(1) as a prohibition rather than a right to be invoked is not anchored to its own paragraphs and remains contested in the literature. Recorded as the designer's reading pending verification.
The prohibition in Art.22 cannot be circumvented by splitting the automated decision across multiple actors (scoring agency + final decision maker). Both may bear responsibility.

Pre-determined assessment criteria may in no circumstances be based on health (PNR Directive Art.6(4); C-817/19 paras 105, 196-197) — a categorical prohibition, not a special-category rule curable by a GDPR Art.9(2) basis. MAILO transposes this to medical AI as a bar on using health condition as a discriminatory classification or risk-scoring criterion, which is narrower than any processing of health data.
Non-transparent, self-learning ML risk assessment systems may not be used for decisions with significant impact. Pre-determined criteria and regular review are required.

Large-scale automated processing must satisfy: (a) targeted scope (C-817/19 paras 167-168, 184, 191), (b) purpose limitation (para 191), (c) temporal limitation (paras 255-256, 262). The Court upheld the PNR Directive subject to Charter-conforming restrictive interpretation; non-conformity at a limb is flagged for review and does not entail invalidity.

comment.en: Data Act. Applies from 2025-09-12. Governs data sharing obligations for IoT-generated data (medical devices, wearables) and B2G/B2B data access for AI development.

Agreement on a Unified Patent Court (in force 2023-06-01). Establishes the UPC as a supranational court for infringement and revocation of European patents across contracting states. Key for medtech AI: opt-out strategy, PI threshold ('more likely than not' invalidity standard from 10x v. NanoString CoA), EPO-UPC divergence risk.

General Data Protection Regulation. Core data protection framework; Art.22 governs solely automated decision-making, Art.15/15(1)(h) the right of access and meaningful information, Art.9 special category health data, Art.35 DPIA obligation.
Data Governance Act. Applies from 2023-09-24. Creates data intermediaries, data altruism organisations, and re-use frameworks for public sector health data.

EU Trade Secrets Directive. Harmonises civil-law protection of undisclosed know-how and business information. Key for medical AI: model weights, training data schemas, and proprietary algorithms qualify as trade secrets under the Art.2 three-part test. Art.5 carve-outs limit the secrecy shield when exercise of the right to information is at stake — directly engaged by GDPR Art.15(1)(h) and AI Act Art.13 transparency obligations.

European Health Data Space. Governs primary use (MyHealth@EU, Art.23) and secondary use (HealthData@EU, Art.75) of health data for research, innovation and AI training. Adopted 11 February 2025, published in the OJ on 5 March 2025, in force 26 March 2025; most secondary-use obligations apply from 26 March 2029, with genetic and clinical-trial data from 26 March 2031. All article references were renumbered in v5.1.0 from COM(2022) 197 proposal numbering to the published text.

European Patent Convention (in force 1977-10-07). Governs patentability of AI/medical-AI inventions (Art.52 exclusions), sufficiency of disclosure for ML models (Art.83), and EPO opposition/appeal proceedings. Administered by EPO; distinct from EU law but intersects via UPC.
Revised Product Liability Directive. AILD was withdrawn 2025-02-10; PLD 2024 is the operative EU strict-liability instrument for AI systems as 'products'.

comment.en: TSD Art.2 protects model weights, training data schemas, and architecture as trade secrets. AI Act Art.13 requires deployers to receive sufficient information about high-risk AI system capabilities and limitations. C-203/22 §§59-62 sets the mandatory floor: controller cannot invoke TSD Art.2 to deny all causal explanation of an automated decision — disputed information must be produced to the competent supervisory authority or court for balance. AI Act Art.78 ensures national authority confidentiality but does not disapply Art.13 disclosure to deployers. TSD Art.5 is the only legislative bridge but its scope in the medical AI context remains unresolved pending a CJEU reference on Art.22 and clinical AI.

labels.en: TSD Art.2 Trade Secret vs. AI Act Art.13 + GDPR Art.15(1)(h) — Core Transparency Tension

comment.en: Article links added in v5.2.0: DataAct Art.4(6)-(8) and Art.5(9)-(11) for the trade-secret limb, AI Act Art.13 and GDPR Art.15(1)(h) for the transparency limb. Note the asymmetry now visible in the graph: Art.13's addressee is the deployer, not the affected person, and Art.86's right to explanation does not reach medical devices on the Annex I route, so on the transparency side only GDPR Art.15(1)(h) actually runs to the individual.

labels.en: Data Act Arts.4(6)-(8) / 5(9)-(11) trade secret vs. AI Act Art.13 + GDPR Art.15(1)(h) transparency

comment.en: EHDS Art.71 grants natural persons a right to opt out of secondary use of their personal electronic health data, enforced by GDPR supervisory authorities. (Renumbered in v5.2.0 from Art.35, which was COM(2022) 197 proposal numbering. The earlier description of the right as 'unconditional' is not verified against the final text and has been removed.) Where opt-out rates are elevated in a clinically significant subpopulation, the resulting training dataset violates AI Act Art.10(3) representativeness. No legislative safe harbour bridges these positions.

labels.en: EHDS Art.71 opt-out vs. AI Act Art.10(3) representativeness

comment.en: PLD Art.10(4) presumes defectiveness and/or the causal link where the claimant faces excessive difficulty owing to technical or scientific complexity and has demonstrated that the defect or link is probable; Art.10(5) preserves the defendant's right to rebut. AI Act Art.9-compliant risk-management documentation may serve to rebut, but no legislative safe harbour confirms this. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the presumption was previously attributed to Art.11, which is exemption from liability.

labels.en: PLD Art.10(4) defect and causation presumption vs. AI Act Art.9 risk management

comment.en: SCOPE NOTE added in v5.2.0: the label and comment conflate patent protection with secrecy. A patent REQUIRES disclosure sufficient to rework the invention (EPC Art.83; see T 161/18 and T 1191/19, which refused AI applications for failing exactly that). It is trade-secret protection, not patent protection, that incentivises withholding model weights. The genuine tension here is between keeping a model opaque and the disclosure that patenting it would require. Needs rewriting before it is cited.

labels.en: Black-Box Patent Protection vs. EU AI Act Transparency Obligation

comment.en: OVERLAP NOTE added in v5.2.0: this tension and Tension_PLD_AIAct_LiabilityGap both concern PLD against AI Act conformity. They are arguably distinct — this one is that conformity assessment is no defence to strict liability (Art.4), the other that risk-management documentation may rebut the Art.10(4) presumption — but the labels do not make the distinction legible and the pair should be merged or renamed before the count of tensions is cited as a contribution.

comment.en: EPO patent prosecution optimises for broad technical-effect claims (wider scope = stronger IP protection); MDR Annex II requires precise intended-purpose specification (narrower scope = easier clinical evaluation); AI Act Art.9/13 requires intermediate characterisation covering intended purpose plus reasonably foreseeable misuse. The same SaMD must be described at opposing granularity levels across three institutional knowledge spaces. No EPO, MDCG, or AI Office guidance addresses this triangular scope alignment problem.

comment.en: DGA Art.12(1)(a) prohibits a data intermediation services provider from using the data it intermediates for purposes other than putting it at the disposal of data users, and requires provision through a separate legal person. Integrated AI development models in which intermediary and developer are related entities therefore require structural separation, which no guidance resolves.

comment.en: Compliance with one framework does not resolve, and may not even bear on, exposure under another liability regime (e.g. AI Act conformity against the revised Product Liability Directive).
Frameworks impose incompatible conditions on the acquisition, sharing or reuse of data (e.g. an EHDS opt-out reducing dataset representativeness against AI Act Art.10 data-quality duties).

Two frameworks impose parallel conformity-assessment routes that neither recognises, so satisfying one does not discharge the other (e.g. MDR notified-body assessment alongside AI Act high-risk conformity assessment).

Frameworks describe the same artefact at incompatible levels of specificity, so a statement that satisfies one reads as over- or under-inclusive under another (e.g. broad EPO claim scope against narrow MDR intended purpose against intermediate AI Act foreseeable use).
A disclosure duty under one framework collides with a legitimate secrecy interest protected by another (TSD Art.2 against AI Act Art.13 and GDPR Art.15(1)(h)).

comment.en:
Software intended to provide information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is Class IIa, rising to Class III where such decisions may cause death or an irreversible deterioration of health, and to Class IIb where they may cause a serious deterioration or surgical intervention. Software intended to monitor physiological processes is Class IIa, or IIb where monitoring vital parameters whose variation could result in immediate danger. All other software is Class I.

This is the linchpin connecting MDR to the AI Act and was absent from MAILO. Rule 11 places most diagnostic and decision-support software at Class IIa or above, which requires notified-body conformity assessment, which in turn makes the system high-risk under AI Act Art.6(1) by the ANNEX I route — and therefore outside the Art.86 right to explanation. The dual-track burden and the Art.86 exclusion both follow from this classification rule. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: MDR Annex VIII Rule 11 — Classification of software

comment.en: Medical device manufacturers must conduct clinical evaluation demonstrating safety and performance. For AI-SaMD, AI-specific performance validation (bias, drift, edge cases) is required.

The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing; a reasonable fee based on administrative costs may be charged for further copies. Interpreted in C-307/22 as requiring a faithful and intelligible reproduction, extending to full documents where necessary to understand the data. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: GDPR Art.15(3) — Right to a copy

comment.en: Manufacturers must designate a person responsible for regulatory compliance (PRRC). For AI-SaMD companies this person must have expertise in medical AI regulation.

labels.en: MDR Art.15 — Person Responsible for Regulatory Compliance

comment.en:
Art.52(1): European patents are granted for any inventions in all fields of technology, provided they are new, involve an inventive step and are susceptible of industrial application. Art.52(2) excludes, among others, mathematical methods and programs for computers; Art.52(3) limits that exclusion to such subject matter 'AS SUCH'.

SCOPE NOTE added in v5.2.0: no MAILO case now interprets this article. All three EPO instances were re-anchored to Arts.56, 83 and 84 after the audit found the Art.52 attribution wrong in each. The provision is retained because the 'as such' limitation is the first hurdle any computer-implemented invention clears — G 1/19 confirms it is passed by any technical means — but it should be understood as background rather than as a provision MAILO's case law turns on.

The technical documentation manufacturers must prepare, beginning at section 1.1 with the device description and specification including intended purpose, intended users and clinical indications. Referenced by Tension_EPO_MDR_SemanticScope, which contrasts the precision MDR demands of the intended purpose with the breadth patent prosecution seeks in claim scope. Added in v5.2.0: the tension cited this annex while the ontology did not encode it.

Inventive step. Basis for the line of authority holding that merely applying a known machine-learning technique to a particular field follows a general technological trend and is not inventive as such (T 161/18 point 3.6; followed in T 1191/19).
Right of access by the data subject.

A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems as a CONTINUOUS ITERATIVE PROCESS planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It comprises identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation of risks in intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and adoption of appropriate targeted risk-management measures. Art.9(10) permits integration with procedures required by other Union harmonisation law, which is the basis for combining it with MDR risk management rather than duplicating it.

labels.en: AI Act Art.9 — Risk management system

comment.en: Secondary use of electronic health data must take place within a secure processing environment under the control of a health data access body, from which raw data cannot be downloaded. This is the medical-domain reconciliation route for the trade-secret / transparency tension: disclosure to a controlled environment rather than to the requester. Implementing acts under Art.73(5) apply from 26 March 2029. Added in v5.1.0.

HealthData@EU connects national contact points for secondary use, enabling EU-wide access to datasets through a single channel without raw data transfer. Not to be confused with MyHealth@EU (Art.23), the corresponding infrastructure for primary use. Third-country participation becomes possible under Art.75(5) from 26 March 2035. Renumbered in v5.1.0: previously recorded as Art.50, which is COM(2022) 197 proposal numbering.

labels.en: EHDS Art.75 — HealthData@EU (cross-border infrastructure for secondary use)

comment.en:
The Directive shall not affect: (a) the exercise of the right to freedom of expression and information as set out in the Charter, including media freedom and pluralism; (b) THE APPLICATION OF UNION OR NATIONAL RULES REQUIRING TRADE SECRET HOLDERS TO DISCLOSE, FOR REASONS OF PUBLIC INTEREST, INFORMATION INCLUDING TRADE SECRETS, TO THE PUBLIC OR TO ADMINISTRATIVE OR JUDICIAL AUTHORITIES FOR THE PERFORMANCE OF THE DUTIES OF THOSE AUTHORITIES; (c) the application of rules requiring or allowing Union institutions and bodies or national public authorities to disclose information submitted by businesses; (d) the autonomy of social partners.

Art.1(2)(b) is the correct doctrinal anchor for the transparency-secrecy interface and had been absent from MAILO, its function having been wrongly attributed to Art.5. It maps directly onto the structure the CJEU adopted in C-203/22 — disclosure to a supervisory authority or court, which then balances — and onto EHDS Art.52, where protected elements are disclosed into an HDAB-controlled environment rather than to the requester. Note the limit it also implies: Art.1(2)(b) preserves disclosure duties owed to authorities and, where the rule so provides, to the public. It does not by itself create a disclosure duty owed to an individual. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: TSD Art.1(2) — Matters the Directive does not affect

comment.en: Deployers, for example a hospital using a third-party system, must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure use in accordance with the instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose so far as they control it (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider of risks or serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers before putting a system into use in the workplace (26(7)); and, where a decision concerning a natural person is taken on the basis of an Annex III system's output, inform the affected person that they are subject to it (26(11)). Note that 26(11), like Art.86, is scoped to Annex III.

labels.en: AI Act Art.26 — Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems

comment.en: Opens Chapter II (Arts 3-9) by fixing the categories of protected data held by public sector bodies whose re-use the Regulation conditions, including data subject to statistical or commercial confidentiality and personal data. The substantive re-use conditions, including anonymisation and the secure processing environment, are in Art.5. Applies to AI training use cases at hospitals and research institutes. Corrected in v5.1.0 Round 5: previously recorded as Art.2, the Definitions article.

labels.en: DGA Art.3 — Categories of protected public sector data eligible for re-use

comment.en: Defines the terms used throughout the Regulation, including 'data', 'data holder', 'data user', 'data intermediation service' at Art.2(11) and 'data altruism'. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: previously labelled 'Re-use of Public Sector Health Data' and described as the Chapter II framework. Chapter II on re-use of protected public sector data runs from Art.3, with the categories at Art.3 and the conditions for re-use at Art.5.
Prohibition on solely automated individual decision-making.
Defines which services fall within the data intermediation regime. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the neutrality obligation previously described here belongs to Art.12; notification is Art.11.

Union or Member State law may restrict the scope of Arts.12-22 where the restriction respects the essence of fundamental rights and is necessary and proportionate. Held in C-307/22 not to permit national law to shift the cost of a first copy onto the data subject in order to protect the controller's economic interests. Added in v5.2.0.

The GSPRs a device must meet. Chapter II section 17 governs electronic programmable systems and software: devices incorporating such systems shall be designed to ensure repeatability, reliability and performance in line with their intended use, software shall be developed and manufactured in accordance with the state of the art taking account of the development lifecycle, risk management including information security, verification and validation. The provision against which AI-specific validation expectations are read. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: MDR Annex I — General safety and performance requirements

comment.en: Art.10 carries BOTH presumptions. Art.10(2): defectiveness is presumed where the defendant fails to disclose evidence, the product does not comply with mandatory safety requirements, or an obvious malfunction occurred. Art.10(4): defectiveness and/or the causal link are presumed where the claimant faces excessive difficulty owing to technical or scientific complexity and has demonstrated that the defect or the link is probable — the limb of most consequence for medical AI, expressly contemplated at recital 48. Art.10(5) preserves the defendant's right to rebut.

labels.en: PLD Art.10 — Burden of proof (presumptions of defectiveness AND of causal link)

comment.en: Natural persons may opt out of the processing of their personal electronic health data for secondary use. GDPR supervisory authorities are competent for monitoring and enforcing this right. Creates tension with AI Act Art.10 data governance obligations, since opt-out reduces dataset representativeness. Renumbered in v5.1.0: previously recorded as Art.35, which is COM(2022) 197 proposal numbering.

labels.en: EHDS Art.71 — Right to opt out of secondary use

comment.en: Grounds on which an economic operator escapes liability, the burden resting on the operator: the product was not placed on the market by them, the defect probably did not exist when the product was placed on the market, or the defect is due to compliance with mandatory legal requirements. The state-of-the-art (development risk) defence sits at Art.11(1)(e), and Member States may derogate from it under Art.18(2). CORRECTED in v5.1.0: this individual previously carried the causation presumption, which is Art.10(4), not Art.11.

Member States shall ensure that any natural person who suffers damage caused by a defective product is entitled to compensation. The strict-liability rule itself: fault need not be shown, only damage, defectiveness and the causal link. Added in v5.2.0, the strict-liability content having previously been attributed to Art.4.

Defines 'product' as all movables, even if integrated into or interconnected with another movable or immovable, including electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and SOFTWARE. The provision that brings standalone software and AI systems within the strict-liability regime, and the basis on which SaMD under the MDR is simultaneously a product under the PLD. Free and open-source software developed or supplied outside a commercial activity is excluded.

CORRECTED in v5.2.0: this individual previously carried the label 'Strict Liability for Defective Products' and the defectiveness test. Strict liability and the right to compensation are Art.5; the test that a product is defective where it does not provide the safety a person is entitled to expect is Art.7. The software-as-product content previously recorded under Art.7 belongs here. The two entries were in effect transposed.

labels.en: PLD Art.4 — Definitions ('product' includes software and AI systems)

comment.en: Member States may put in place organisational or technical arrangements to facilitate data altruism. Registration of recognised data altruism organisations, which may collect health data voluntarily shared for AI research, is governed by Arts.18-19; such entities are separate from commercial data intermediation services. Scope clarified in v5.1.0: the earlier label attributed the registration regime to Art.16.

labels.en: DGA Art.16 — National arrangements for data altruism

comment.en: Where a public sector body, the Commission, the ECB or a Union body demonstrates an exceptional need under Art.15, the data holder shall make the data available. The obligation Art.15 qualifies and Art.17 procedurally implements. Added in v5.2.0: MAILO recorded the Chapter V machinery without the provision that creates the duty.

labels.en: Data Act Art.14 — Obligation to make data available on the basis of exceptional need

comment.en: The cross-border infrastructure for primary use, to be distinguished from HealthData@EU at Art.75, which serves secondary use. Added in v5.2.0 because the two were previously conflatable: the superseded Art.50 entry described HealthData@EU using proposal numbering with no primary-use counterpart recorded.

labels.en: EHDS Art.23 — MyHealth@EU (cross-border infrastructure for PRIMARY use)

comment.en: Health data access bodies issue data permits authorising secondary use of electronic health data for research, innovation and policy. Access is granted within a secure processing environment (Art.73) from which raw data cannot be downloaded; a health data request under Art.69 yields only an anonymised statistical answer. Renumbered in v5.1.0: previously recorded as Art.33, which is COM(2022) 197 proposal numbering.

labels.en: EHDS Art.68 — Data permit (secondary use authorisation)

comment.en: Where a health data user seeks only an answer in anonymised statistical form, a health data request may be made instead of a data permit; the HDAB supplies the result rather than access to the underlying data. The least intrusive route in the access hierarchy and a candidate safeguard where a protected element under Art.52 cannot be adequately mitigated within a secure processing environment. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: EHDS Art.69 — Health data request (anonymised statistical answer)

comment.en: Art.12(1)(a): the provider shall not use the data for which it provides intermediation services for purposes other than putting them at the disposal of data users, and shall provide the service through a separate legal person. Art.12(1)(c) restricts use of activity metadata to service development. Added in v5.2.0 to carry the neutrality obligation previously misattributed to Art.10.

labels.en: DGA Art.12 — Conditions for providing data intermediation services (neutrality)

comment.en: Defines when a public sector body has an exceptional need justifying a request for data under Chapter V. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: this individual was labelled 'Trade Secret Protection'. The Data Act's trade-secret safeguards are in Art.4(6)-(8) (data holder to user) and Art.5(9)-(11) (user to third party), not Art.15.

labels.en: Data Act Art.15 — Exceptional need to use data (B2G)

comment.en: High-risk AI providers must implement a QMS covering design, development, post-market monitoring. Aligned with MDR Annex IX QMS requirements to avoid double burden.

labels.en: AI Act Art.17 — Quality Management System

comment.en: Information and action under Arts.15-22 are provided free of charge; a reasonable fee or refusal is possible only for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, and the controller bears the burden of showing this. Basis, with Art.15(3), for the first-copy holding in C-307/22. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: GDPR Art.12(5) — Exercise of data subject rights free of charge

comment.en: MAILO OPERATIONALISATION: continuous monitoring of model drift and performance degradation in deployment populations is the designer's reading of what PMS entails for AI-SaMD. Art.83 requires a post-market surveillance system proportionate to risk class and device type; it does not name drift. Recorded as such in v5.2.0.

A product is defective where it does not provide the safety that a person is entitled to expect or that is required under Union or national law. The assessment takes account of all circumstances, including presentation and instructions, reasonably foreseeable use and misuse, the effect of the ability to continue to learn or of software updates after placing on the market, the moment in time at which the product was placed on the market or remained within the manufacturer's control, and relevant product safety requirements including cybersecurity.

CORRECTED in v5.2.0: previously labelled 'AI and Software as Products' and describing the product definition, which is Art.4. The continued-learning limb recorded here is the provision on which MAILO's model-drift arguments actually rest.

The recoverable heads of damage: death or personal injury including medically recognised harm to psychological health; damage to or destruction of property other than the defective product itself, excluding property used exclusively for professional purposes; and destruction or corruption of data not used for professional purposes. Added in v5.2.0.
Courts may order defendants to disclose evidence about high-risk AI systems; creates procedural discovery mechanism absent in AILD.

Art.10(3): training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, TO THE BEST EXTENT POSSIBLE, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier comment listed 'freedom from errors, completeness' as flat criteria, dropping the qualifier the final text added precisely because absolute error-freedom is unattainable. The distinction matters for any claim that a dataset defect breaches Art.10(3) — including Tension_EHDS_GDPR_OptOut, which asserts that elevated opt-out rates in a clinically significant subpopulation put a dataset in violation. Under the qualified standard that conclusion requires showing the shortfall was avoidable, not merely that it exists.

labels.en: AI Act Art.10 — Data and data governance

comment.en: Three-part cumulative test: information must be (1) secret (not generally known or readily accessible), (2) have commercial value because it is secret, and (3) be subject to reasonable steps to keep it secret. All three must hold for ML model weights or training data to qualify.

labels.en: TSD Article 2 — Definition of Trade Secret

comment.en:
Art.13(1): high-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable DEPLOYERS to interpret the output and use it appropriately. Art.13(2)-(3): instructions for use must accompany the system, specifying provider identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance including accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity metrics, known foreseeable risks, human oversight measures and expected lifetime.

SCOPE NOTE added in v5.2.0: the addressee is the DEPLOYER, not the affected person. Art.13 confers nothing on a patient or data subject. This is the pivot of the trade-secret debate — a provider may satisfy Art.13 in full while an affected individual receives nothing, which is why the explanation route for individuals runs through GDPR Art.15(1)(h) and Art.22, and, in the health domain, through EHDS Art.52's controlled-access mechanism. The earlier one-line comment did not record the addressee distinction on which that argument depends.

labels.en: AI Act Art.13 — Transparency and provision of information TO DEPLOYERS

comment.en: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during use, including through appropriate human-machine interface tools. Oversight measures aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and must enable the person to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret output, disregard or override it, and intervene or stop the system. The complementedBy link to GDPR Art.22(3) should be read subject to the note on that article: the Art.22(3) safeguards attach only to Art.22(2)(a) and (c), so oversight under Art.14 and the data-protection safeguards do not automatically coincide.

Everyone has the right to respect for his or her private and family life, home and communications. Together with Art.8 the constitutional basis against which the Court assessed the PNR Directive in C-817/19 and the retention regimes in C-511/18.

labels.en: EU Charter Art.7 — Respect for private and family life

comment.en:
The procedural requirements for a request under Chapter V: what the request must specify, and the cross-border route under Art.17(3) by which a public sector body intending to request data from a holder established in another Member State must first notify that Member State's competent authority designated under Art.37, which then examines the request against Art.17.

CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier entry described Art.17 as 'B2G Data Sharing (Public Emergency)', asserting that governments may require medical AI companies to share health data in a public health emergency. Public emergency is a ground of exceptional need under Art.15, not the subject of Art.17. Art.14 states the obligation itself. The substantive claim about epidemic surveillance AI therefore rested on the wrong provision.

labels.en: Data Act Art.17 — Requests by public sector bodies for data to be made available

comment.en: Everyone has the right to the protection of personal data concerning him or her; such data must be processed fairly, for specified purposes and on a legitimate basis laid down by law; everyone has the right of access to data collected concerning them and the right to have it rectified; and compliance is subject to control by an independent authority. Art.8(2) is the Charter root of the GDPR Art.15 access right that C-203/22 and C-307/22 interpret; Art.8(3) is the independent-supervision requirement echoed in C-817/19 paras 222-227.

labels.en: EU Charter Art.8 — Protection of personal data

comment.en: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

Courts may impose confidentiality measures to protect trade secrets during litigation. Relevant to UPC discovery proceedings where a party seeks disclosure of AI model architecture or training data as part of infringement or validity analysis.

labels.en: TSD Article 9 — Preservation of Confidentiality in Legal Proceedings

comment.en: Transparency duties on providers and deployers of AI systems that interact with natural persons or generate synthetic audio, image, video or text, including machine-readable marking and disclosure of artificially generated content. Applies to AI-generated radiology reports and diagnostic summaries. Relabelled in v5.1.0: this is NOT the GPAI regime, which is Chapter V (Arts.51-56) and addresses providers of general-purpose AI models.

labels.en: AI Act Art.50 — Transparency obligations for certain AI systems

comment.en:
Connected products shall be designed and manufactured, and connected services designed and provided, so that product data and related service data are, by default, directly accessible to the user in a simple, secure, free-of-charge, comprehensive, structured, commonly used and machine-readable format. Art.3(2)-(3) add pre-contractual information duties covering the nature, format and estimated volume of the data, whether it is generated in real time, and where it is stored. Applies to products placed on the market from 12 September 2026.

CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier entry described Art.3 as an 'IoT Data Access Right ... enforceable against manufacturers'. That is Art.4. Art.3 is a design and by-default-accessibility obligation; the user's right to obtain data from the data holder is separate and has applied since 12 September 2025. For connected medical devices the distinction is practical, not merely formal: a device placed on the market before September 2026 is outside the design duty while its holder is already subject to the access duty.

labels.en: Data Act Art.3 — Obligation to make product data accessible BY DESIGN

comment.en: Acquisition is lawful where obtained by independent discovery or creation, or by observation, study, disassembly or testing of a product or object that has been made available to the public or is lawfully in the possession of the acquirer who is free of any legally valid duty to limit the acquisition — that is, REVERSE ENGINEERING is lawful acquisition unless contractually excluded. Directly relevant to medical AI: analysing a deployed model's behaviour through observation and testing is not an unlawful acquisition of the trade secrets it embodies, which bears on both explainability research and the practical reach of secrecy over deployed systems. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: TSD Art.3 — Lawful acquisition, use and disclosure

comment.en:
Art.4(1): where data is not directly accessible from the connected product, data holders shall make readily available data, and the relevant metadata, available to the user without undue delay, in the same quality as it is available to the data holder, easily, securely, free of charge and in a machine-readable format. Art.4(4): data holders shall not unreasonably impede the user's choices or rights through the structure, design, function or operation of a digital user interface.

Art.4(6)-(8) carry the trade-secret safeguards: trade secrets are disclosed to the user only where the holder and user agree the measures necessary to preserve confidentiality; the holder may withhold or suspend sharing where it demonstrates that it is highly likely to suffer serious economic damage, with notification to the competent authority. This is the Data Act limb of MAILO's trade-secret-against-transparency tension, and it is a qualified withholding right rather than a veto. Scope broadened in v5.2.0: the entry previously covered only paragraphs (6)-(8).

labels.en: Data Act Art.4 — Rights and obligations of users and data holders regarding access and use

comment.en:
An application for the measures, procedures and remedies is dismissed where the acquisition, use or disclosure was carried out (a) for exercising the right to freedom of expression and information as set out in the Charter, including respect for the freedom and pluralism of the media; (b) for revealing misconduct, wrongdoing or illegal activity in order to protect the general public interest; (c) by workers to their representatives in the legitimate exercise of representative functions; or (d) for the purpose of protecting a legitimate interest recognised by Union or national law.

CORRECTED in v5.2.0, and this was a substantive error rather than a citation slip. The earlier entry read that trade secret protection does not apply 'where disclosure is required for the exercise of the right to information', and treated Art.5 as the provision engaged when a data subject invokes GDPR Art.15(1)(h). Art.5(a) is the freedom of expression and information of Charter Art.11 — media freedom, investigative journalism, protection of journalistic sources per recital 19. A patient seeking an explanation of an automated medical decision is not exercising that right. Art.5(d) might be argued to cover data-protection rights as a legitimate interest recognised by Union law, but that is an argument to be made rather than a plain reading, and the CJEU did not take that route in C-203/22: the Court resolved the trade-secret defence within the GDPR itself, requiring disclosure to the supervisory authority or court for balancing. The provision that actually preserves regulatory disclosure duties is Art.1(2)(b), now encoded separately.

labels.en: TSD Art.5 — Exceptions (freedom of expression, whistleblowing, workers' representatives, legitimate interest)

comment.en: Data holders must share IoT-generated health data with third parties at user request. Creates AI training data supply chain implications for medical device manufacturers.

labels.en: Data Act Art.5 — Data Sharing with Third Parties

comment.en: Lists what health data holders must make available: EHR data, data on factors influencing health, pathogen data, healthcare-related administrative and claims data, human genetic, epigenomic and genomic data, other molecular omics data, automatically generated personal EHD from medical devices, data from wellness applications, health-professional and health-facility data, population-based health-data registries, health-data registries and clinical-trial data. Art.51(h) and (n) in particular govern device-generated data, where industry commentary argues the scope should reach only processed human-readable information rather than raw machine data used internally to derive diagnostic scores. Added in v5.2.0.

labels.en: EHDS Art.51 — Minimum categories of electronic health data for secondary use

comment.en: A public sector body, the Commission, the ECB or a Union body may share data received under Chapter V with individuals or organisations conducting scientific research or analytics compatible with the purpose of the request, or with national statistical institutes and Eurostat. Recipients assume the obligations in Art.17(3) and Art.19, and organisations under significant commercial influence likely to result in preferential access to results are excluded. Relevant to medical-AI research using data obtained through the exceptional-need route. Added in v5.2.0.

comment.en: The provision governing the trade-secret / access conflict in the health domain, and the one most directly relevant to MAILO's transparency-secrecy tension. Datasets protected by IP rights, trade secrets or regulatory data protection may still be made available for secondary use provided the health data holder identifies and substantiates the protected elements. The health data access body must then take all specific, appropriate and proportionate legal, organisational and technical measures, which may include contractual arrangements, and may refuse access where a serious risk of infringement cannot be addressed satisfactorily. Art.52(3) covers technical measures. The decision chain it leaves to be operationalised runs: protected element, substantiated claim, access scenario, infringement pathway, safeguard, residual risk, permit or conditional permit or refusal. Added in v5.2.0: MAILO had encoded five EHDS articles and omitted this one.

comment.en: In the cases referred to in POINTS (a) AND (c) of Art.22(2), the controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the controller's part, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier text said these safeguards apply whenever an exception applies. They do NOT attach to point (b): where the basis is Union or Member State law, that law must itself lay down suitable measures. The distinction is material for medical AI operating on a national legal basis, where the Art.22(3) triad cannot simply be assumed.

Health data access bodies may grant access to Art.51 data only where processing is necessary for one of the listed purposes: public interest in public and occupational health; policy-making and regulatory activities; official statistics; education and training in the health or care sector; and scientific research related to health or care that contributes to public health or health technology assessment or ensures high quality and safety of healthcare, medicinal products or medical devices.

Art.53(1)(e)(ii) is of first-order importance to MAILO and was previously absent: it expressly names 'training, testing and evaluation of algorithms, INCLUDING IN MEDICAL DEVICES, IN VITRO DIAGNOSTIC MEDICAL DEVICES, AI SYSTEMS AND DIGITAL HEALTH APPLICATIONS' as a permitted secondary-use purpose. This is the express legal pathway for training medical AI on EHDS data, and the point at which the AI Act Art.10 data-governance duties and the EHDS access regime meet. Added in v5.2.0.

comment.en: The data subject shall have the RIGHT NOT TO BE SUBJECT to a decision based solely on automated processing, INCLUDING PROFILING, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier text read 'individuals shall not be subject to', stating a flat prohibition. Whether Art.22(1) is a prohibition applying of its own force or a right the data subject must invoke is contested and was not settled by C-634/21 — see the note on P_634_004. The encoding now follows the wording of the provision rather than pre-committing to one reading. The earlier text also omitted profiling and compressed the two-limb effects test.

comment.en: The data subject has the right to be informed of THE EXISTENCE of automated decision-making, including profiling, REFERRED TO IN ART.22(1) AND (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing. Interpreted in C-203/22 paras 59-62. CORRECTED in v5.2.0: the earlier text omitted both the existence limb and the cross-reference scoping this right to Art.22(1) and (4) cases, which is what ties the explanation duty to the automated-decision regime rather than to processing at large.

comment.en:
An affected person subject to a decision taken by a deployer on the basis of the output of a high-risk AI system LISTED IN ANNEX III, excluding systems under point 2, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them adversely in health, safety or fundamental rights, may obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision. Art.86(2) disapplies it where Union or national law provides exceptions; Art.86(3) makes it residual to rights available elsewhere in Union law.

SCOPE WARNING added in v5.2.0, and consequential for MAILO's domain: AI-based medical devices are high-risk by the ANNEX I route under Art.6(1), because MDR and IVDR are listed in Annex I Section A and Class IIa/IIb/III devices require third-party conformity assessment. Annex I is not Annex III. Art.86 therefore does NOT confer a right to explanation in respect of a diagnostic or imaging AI device that is high-risk solely as a regulated medical device. It can apply to healthcare AI reaching high-risk status through Annex III point 5, such as systems determining eligibility for publicly funded healthcare services. For the Annex I population, GDPR Art.15(1)(h) and Art.22 carry the explanation duty alone. The previous complementedBy link to GDPR Art.15(1)(h) implied the two operate together across medical AI; it is retained but qualified by this note.
